title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
summary: Chemistry begins when one substance changes into another with entirely new properties. This chapter teaches how to write chemical equations and balance them so that atoms obey the law of conservation of mass, and how to add physical states and reaction conditions to make equations fully informative. Reactions are then classified into combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement and redox types using laboratory examples such as burning magnesium, heating ferrous sulphate crystals, electrolysis of water, the iron nail dipped in copper sulphate solution and the white precipitate of barium sulphate. Energy changes divide reactions into exothermic ones like respiration, combustion and slaking of quicklime, and endothermic ones like decomposition of limestone. The chapter closes with two unwanted effects of oxidation in daily life: corrosion, which eats up surfaces of iron, copper and silver, and rancidity, which spoils the taste and smell of fatty food, along with practical methods such as galvanisation, antioxidants and nitrogen flushing used to prevent them.
hotTopics: Physical states and reaction conditions in equations
Identifying oxidation, reduction and redox pairs
Corrosion of iron, copper and silver

sections.heading: Writing and Balancing Chemical Equations
sections.para: A chemical equation is the shorthand language of chemistry. A complete word equation like zinc plus sulphuric acid gives zinc sulphate plus hydrogen is first converted into a formula equation: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2. The substances that enter the reaction, written on the left of the arrow, are reactants; the new substances formed on the right are products. A correct equation must obey the law of conservation of mass, which says matter can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, so the number of atoms of every element must be equal on both sides. An equation that merely lists formulae without equalising atoms is called a skeletal equation. Balancing is done by hit and trial, adjusting only the coefficients written in front of formulae, never the formulae themselves, until atoms of each element match on the two sides.
points: A chemical equation represents a reaction using symbols and formulae: reactants on the left, products on the right, joined by an arrow that points towards the products.
The arrow head means gives or produces; it also shows the direction of the change.
A balanced equation has equal numbers of atoms of each element on both sides and therefore obeys the law of conservation of mass.
A skeletal equation is unbalanced; it is converted to a balanced equation by hit and trial changing only coefficients.
Burning of magnesium ribbon in air: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, a combination reaction with a dazzling white flame forming white magnesium oxide powder.
Zinc granules in dilute sulphuric acid: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2; the hydrogen gas burns with a pop sound.
Common mistake: multiplying atoms inside a formula while balancing, e.g. writing MgO2 for 2MgO, which changes the substance itself.

keyTerms.meaning: Symbolic representation of a chemical reaction using formulae of reactants and products.
The starting substance written on the left side of the arrow in a chemical equation.
The new substance formed and written on the right side of the arrow.
An equation with equal atom counts of every element on both sides, obeying conservation of mass.
An unbalanced equation that only lists the formulae of reactants and products.
The number written in front of a formula during balancing; it multiplies the whole formula.

sections.trick: Balance in the order M-N-H-O: Metals, then Non-metals, then Hydrogen, then Oxygen last. Change only the numbers in front of formulae, never the formulae themselves.
sections.examPointer: Balancing a given equation and naming reactants and products is a guaranteed 2-3 mark question; one balancing item usually also hides inside case-based questions.

sections.heading: Making Equations More Informative: States and Conditions
sections.para: A fully informative equation tells not only what reacts but also the physical states of the substances and the conditions under which the reaction happens. Symbols in brackets after each formula do this work: (s) for solid, (l) for liquid, (g) for gas and (aq) for a substance dissolved in water, that is an aqueous solution. Thus the reaction of iron with steam is written as 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g), where water is in the gaseous state because steam is used. Conditions such as heat, a catalyst, pressure or sunlight, if needed, are written above or below the arrow. For example, the decomposition of silver chloride needs sunlight, and the decomposition of water needs an electric current, so these are indicated along the arrow. Such details make the equation a complete record of the reaction.
points: Physical state symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) aqueous solution, written immediately after each formula.
Iron with steam: 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g); hydrogen evolved burns with a pop sound.
When a gas like hydrogen is collected in a test tube and a burning candle is brought near, the pop sound confirms hydrogen.
Conditions like heat, catalyst, pressure or sunlight are written on or beside the arrow, e.g. sunlight over the arrow in 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2.
The calcium oxide reaction is written with water as a liquid: CaO(s) + H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq), showing slaked lime forms in solution.
Precipitates formed in solution are marked (s) while the remaining dissolved salts are marked (aq).

keyTerms.meaning: Bracketed letter (s), (l), (g) or (aq) showing the state of each substance in an equation.
A solution in which the solute is dissolved in water, indicated by (aq).
Requirement such as heat, catalyst or sunlight written along the arrow in an equation.
A substance that changes the rate of a reaction without itself being consumed.

sections.trick: Read state brackets as a story: s is solid stuff, l is liquid, g is gas, aq is dissolved in water. If the arrow needs help, heat, catalyst or sunlight sit on top of it.
sections.examPointer: Writing state symbols for a given equation carries 1-2 marks; questions also ask why steam is shown as H2O(g) rather than H2O(l).

sections.heading: Combination Reactions
sections.para: In a combination reaction two or more reactants join to form a single product, so the general pattern is A + B -> AB. Burning of coal, C + O2 -> CO2, and formation of water from hydrogen and oxygen are simple examples. The most memorable school example is slaking of quicklime: when calcium oxide is added to water in a bucket, it combines to give calcium hydroxide, CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, releasing so much heat that the container becomes hot. The milky suspension of slaked lime is used for whitewashing walls; after two or three days it reacts with carbon dioxide of the air to form a thin shiny layer of calcium carbonate, Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O, giving the wall a glossy finish. Many combination reactions are exothermic because bonds formed release energy.
points: General form: A + B -> AB; two or more substances give a single new substance.
Quicklime slaking: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + heat; a highly exothermic combination reaction used for whitewashing.
Slaked lime slowly reacts with atmospheric carbon dioxide: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O, giving walls a shiny white finish.
Burning of coal: C + O2 -> CO2, and formation of water: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, are combination reactions releasing heat and light.
Iron and sulphur combine on heating: Fe + S -> FeS, forming black iron sulphide.
Calcium oxide is called quicklime, calcium hydroxide slaked lime, and calcium carbonate limestone or marble in its natural form.

keyTerms.meaning: A reaction in which two or more reactants combine to form a single product.
Calcium oxide, CaO, obtained by heating limestone.
Calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2, formed when water is added to quicklime.
Application of slaked lime suspension on walls, which slowly turns into shiny calcium carbonate.

sections.trick: Combination marries many into one: A plus B equals AB. Quicklime plus water is the hot white pair behind every whitewashed wall.
sections.examPointer: The two whitewashing equations with labels of quicklime and slaked lime are a favourite 3-marker; identifying a reaction as combination plus exothermic is common in MCQs.

sections.heading: Decomposition Reactions: Heat, Light and Electricity
sections.para: A decomposition reaction is the exact opposite of combination: a single substance breaks down into two or more simpler substances, AB -> A + B. Energy in some form must always be supplied. Thermal decomposition uses heat: limestone splits as CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, and pale green ferrous sulphate crystals lose water and then break as 2FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3, the solid turning brown with the smell of burning sulphur. Heating lead nitrate gives brown nitrogen dioxide fumes: 2Pb(NO3)2 -> 2PbO + 4NO2 + O2. Electrolytic decomposition uses electricity: passing current through acidified water gives 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2, with hydrogen collected in double the volume of oxygen. Photolytic decomposition uses light: white silver chloride turns grey as 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2, the basis of black and white photography; silver bromide behaves similarly.
points: General form: AB -> A + B; energy in the form of heat, light or electricity is always absorbed.
Thermal decomposition of limestone: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 on heating; used in cement and lime industry.
Heating ferrous sulphate crystals: 2FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3; green crystals turn brown and smell of burning sulphur.
Heating lead nitrate: 2Pb(NO3)2 -> 2PbO + 4NO2 + O2; brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide evolve.
Electrolysis of acidified water: 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2; hydrogen at cathode is double the volume of oxygen at anode.
Photolytic decomposition: 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 and 2AgBr -> 2Ag + Br2 in sunlight; white salts turn grey, used in photography.
All decomposition reactions that absorb heat are endothermic, so energy appears as a reactant.

keyTerms.meaning: Breaking of a single compound into two or more simpler substances using heat, light or electricity.
Decomposition brought about by heating, e.g. limestone to quicklime.
Decomposition caused by passing electricity, e.g. water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Decomposition caused by light, e.g. silver chloride turning grey in sunlight.

sections.trick: ETP breaks compounds: Electricity, Thermal, Photolytic. Green FeSO4 turns brown with burning-sulphur smell; AgCl fears sunlight and turns grey like an old photograph.
sections.examPointer: Heating of ferrous sulphate, silver chloride and lead nitrate with colour and smell observations is repeatedly asked as 2-3 mark questions and in assertion-reason items.

sections.heading: Displacement Reactions
sections.para: In a displacement reaction a more reactive element pushes a less reactive element out of its compound and takes its place: A + BC -> AC + B. The classic experiment is dipping an iron nail in copper sulphate solution. Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces it: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. The blue colour of the solution fades to light green as ferrous sulphate forms, and a brown coating of copper deposits on the nail. Similarly zinc displaces copper, Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu, while copper cannot displace zinc, proving Zn is more reactive. Copper does displace silver: Cu + 2AgNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag, giving the order Zn > Cu > Ag. Lead also displaces copper from copper chloride solution: Pb + CuCl2 -> PbCl2 + Cu. Such reactions establish the reactivity order of metals.
points: General form: A + BC -> AC + B; the more reactive element takes the place of the less reactive one.
Iron nail in copper sulphate: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu; blue solution turns light green and brown copper deposits on the nail.
Zinc in copper sulphate: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu; but copper cannot displace zinc from zinc sulphate, showing Zn > Cu.
Copper in silver nitrate: Cu + 2AgNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag; solution turns blue and shining silver deposits, so Cu > Ag.
Lead in copper chloride: Pb + CuCl2 -> PbCl2 + Cu; lead chloride forms and copper is set free.
Comparing such results gives the activity order, for example Zn > Cu > Ag, which predicts which displacements will occur.
Non-metals also show displacement, e.g. chlorine displaces bromine: Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2.

keyTerms.meaning: A reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.
Arrangement of elements by their ability to displace one another, e.g. Zn > Cu > Ag.
The salt of the displacing element plus the free displaced element, e.g. FeSO4 and Cu.

sections.trick: The reactive bully throws the weak one out of its compound house. Watch the colours: blue copper sulphate turns light green with iron, and brown copper parks on the nail.
sections.examPointer: Colour change questions (blue to light green, brown deposit) and predicting whether a displacement will occur are standard 2-3 markers and MCQs almost every year.

sections.heading: Double Displacement and Precipitation Reactions
sections.para: In a double displacement reaction two compounds in solution exchange their ions to form two new compounds: AB + CD -> AD + CB. Mixing sodium sulphate solution with barium chloride solution gives white barium sulphate: Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl. Because BaSO4 is insoluble, it separates out as a fine solid called a precipitate, and any reaction that produces such an insoluble solid is a precipitation reaction. Another beautiful example is lead nitrate with potassium iodide: Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI -> PbI2 + 2KNO3, where a brilliant yellow precipitate of lead iodide appears instantly. When an acid reacts with a base, the ions exchanged are H+ and OH-, forming salt and water; this neutralisation is also a double displacement reaction and is accompanied by evolution of heat. Gas evolution reactions, like carbonates with acids, also involve ion exchange.
points: General form: AB + CD -> AD + CB; the two reacting compounds swap their ions in solution.
Sodium sulphate with barium chloride: Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl; insoluble white BaSO4 is the precipitate.
Lead nitrate with potassium iodide: Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI -> PbI2 + 2KNO3; a yellow precipitate of lead iodide forms at once.
A precipitation reaction is any double displacement reaction that produces an insoluble solid called a precipitate.
Neutralisation, acid + base -> salt + water, is a double displacement reaction accompanied by heat evolution.
Carbonates with acids release carbon dioxide, e.g. Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2, a gas evolution double displacement reaction.

keyTerms.meaning: A reaction in which two compounds exchange ions to form two new compounds.
An insoluble solid that separates out of a solution during a reaction.
Any reaction producing a precipitate, e.g. white BaSO4 or yellow PbI2.
Reaction between an acid and a base giving salt and water; also a double displacement process.

sections.trick: In double displacement the ion partners swap seats like passengers changing coaches; the odd combination falls out as a precipitate, and remember BaSO4 lands white while PbI2 lands yellow.
sections.examPointer: Writing equations for precipitation reactions and naming the colour of the precipitate is a repeated 2-3 marker; one such equation often appears in case-based questions.

sections.heading: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
sections.para: Chemical reactions are always accompanied by energy changes. Reactions in which heat is released along with the products are exothermic; the container feels hot. Burning of natural gas, CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, burning of magnesium, and the slaking of quicklime are exothermic. Respiration is also exothermic: inside cells, glucose combines with oxygen, C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy, and this energy keeps us alive. The slow decomposition of vegetable matter into compost releases heat as well. On the other hand, reactions that absorb heat from the surroundings are endothermic; the mixture turns cold or needs continuous heating. Decomposition of limestone, CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, needs heat; mixing barium hydroxide with ammonium chloride in a test tube drops the temperature so much that the tube freezes to a wooden block; electrolysis of water needs electrical energy.
points: Exothermic reaction: heat is evolved, e.g. burning of natural gas CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O.
Respiration is exothermic: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy; glucose is slowly burnt inside cells to release usable energy.
Dissolving quicklime in water and decomposition of vegetable matter into compost are other exothermic examples.
Endothermic reaction: heat is absorbed, e.g. CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 on heating, and electrolysis of water using electrical energy.
Barium hydroxide mixed with ammonium chloride absorbs heat so fast that the test tube feels freezing cold.
Photosynthesis is endothermic in the broad sense because plants absorb light energy to make glucose.
Most combination reactions are exothermic while most decomposition reactions are endothermic.

keyTerms.meaning: A reaction in which heat is released to the surroundings, e.g. combustion and respiration.
A reaction in which heat is absorbed from the surroundings, e.g. thermal decomposition of limestone.
Exothermic oxidation of glucose in living cells releasing energy for life processes.
Decomposed organic matter; its formation releases heat, showing decomposition of biomass is exothermic.

sections.trick: EXO exits heat so hands get hot; ENDO enters heat so hands get cold. Burning and respiration are twin exothermic processes; barium hydroxide plus ammonium chloride is the classic freezer reaction.
sections.examPointer: Classify given reactions as exothermic or endothermic with reasons (2-3 marks) is asked repeatedly; respiration as an exothermic reaction is a standing CBSE favourite.

sections.heading: Oxidation, Reduction and Redox Reactions
sections.para: Oxidation means gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen by a substance, while reduction means loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen. In most reactions the two happen together, so the reaction is called a redox reaction. When hydrogen gas is passed over hot black copper oxide, the black coating turns brown: CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O. Here CuO loses oxygen, so it is reduced to copper, while H2 gains oxygen, so it is oxidised to water. In ZnO + C -> Zn + CO2, carbon removes oxygen from zinc oxide, so carbon is the reducing agent and ZnO is reduced. Similarly in MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2, MnO2 is reduced and HCl is oxidised to chlorine. The rule to remember: the substance that gets oxidised reduces the other and is called the reducing agent, and the one that gets reduced is the oxidising agent.
points: Oxidation: gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen; reduction: loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen.
CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O: CuO is reduced (black to brown copper), H2 is oxidised to water; a classic redox reaction.
Heating copper powder in air: 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO; the brown copper surface becomes coated with black copper oxide.
ZnO + C -> Zn + CO2: carbon is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent; ZnO is the oxidising agent here.
MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2: HCl loses hydrogen to become Cl2, so HCl is oxidised and MnO2 reduced.
SO2 + 2H2S -> 3S + 2H2O: sulphur dioxide is reduced to sulphur while hydrogen sulphide is oxidised.
Substance oxidised = reducing agent; substance reduced = oxidising agent; both always occur together in redox.

keyTerms.meaning: Gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen by a substance during a reaction.
Loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen by a substance during a reaction.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction take place simultaneously.
The substance that supplies oxygen (or accepts electrons) and itself gets reduced.
The substance that removes oxygen (or supplies electrons) and itself gets oxidised.

sections.trick: Gain O or lose H means oxidised; lose O or gain H means reduced. The oxidised one is the reducing agent because it hands oxygen over, and both always travel together as REDOX.
sections.examPointer: Identify the substance oxidised, the substance reduced and the agents in a given equation; this is a repeated 2-3 marker and a common case-based sub-question.

sections.heading: Corrosion of Metals
sections.para: Corrosion is the slow eating up of metal surfaces by the action of air, moisture or chemicals present around them. Silver articles become black after some time because they react with sulphur in the air to form a coating of silver sulphide. Copper reacts with moist carbon dioxide and gains a green coating of basic copper carbonate. Iron rusts most familiarly: rust forms only when iron is in contact with both air and moisture together, producing a brown flaky substance called hydrated iron(III) oxide, written as Fe2O3.xH2O, where x is the number of water molecules that varies. Rust is soft and crumbles off, exposing fresh metal again, so rusting eats deep into iron bodies of railings, bridges, car bodies and ship hulls and causes enormous annual loss. Prevention includes painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising with zinc, chrome plating, anodising and making alloys like stainless steel.
points: Corrosion: gradual destruction of a metal surface by gases and moisture in the atmosphere.
Rusting of iron requires both air and moisture together; the product is brown flaky hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3.xH2O.
Copper gets a green coating of basic copper carbonate on reaction with moist carbon dioxide of air.
Silver gets a black coating of silver sulphide by reaction with sulphur compounds in the air.
Other metals like aluminium form their own thin oxide layer, Al2O3, which sticks firmly and protects the metal below.
Prevention methods: painting, oiling, greasing, galvanisation (zinc coating), chrome plating, anodising and alloying to stainless steel.
Corrosion damages railings, bridges, ships and car bodies, causing huge annual economic loss.

keyTerms.meaning: Eating away of a metal surface by air, moisture or chemicals in the environment.
Corrosion of iron in the presence of both oxygen and water forming Fe2O3.xH2O.
Coating of iron or steel with a thin layer of zinc to prevent rusting.
The brown flaky composition of rust, Fe2O3 combined with variable water, Fe2O3.xH2O.

sections.trick: Rust needs air plus water together, just as tea needs milk plus water. For coatings remember silver turns black (sulphide) and copper turns green (carbonate).
sections.examPointer: Conditions for rusting, colour and formula of coatings on silver and copper, and methods of prevention are regular MCQs; corrosion is a common case-based theme worth 4-5 marks.

sections.heading: Rancidity and Its Prevention
sections.para: When fats and oils in food are kept for a long time and exposed to air, they get oxidised slowly. This oxidation changes their taste and smell, and the food is said to have become rancid; the process is called rancidity. Chips packets are flushed with the unreactive gas nitrogen before sealing, precisely to push oxygen out and stop the fats from oxidising. At home, rancidity is checked by storing food in airtight containers, keeping it in a refrigerator, keeping it away from sunlight, and adding substances called antioxidants like BHA or BHT that themselves oxidise first and protect the food. Frying in fresh oil, avoiding moisture and using suitable packaging also help. Rancidity and corrosion together show how the gentle process of oxidation, useful in respiration, becomes a nuisance when it attacks our food and our metals.
points: Rancidity: oxidation of fats and oils in food on exposure to air, changing their taste and smell.
Chips packets are puffed with nitrogen gas because nitrogen is unreactive and displaces oxygen, preventing oxidation of the oil.
Antioxidants such as BHA and BHT are added to packaged food; they oxidise first and protect the fats.
Storing food in airtight containers limits contact with atmospheric oxygen and slows rancidity.
Refrigeration lowers the temperature and hence the rate of the oxidation reactions.
Keeping food away from light and moisture further slows oxidation, so cool dark places preserve food better.

keyTerms.meaning: Oxidation of fats and oils in food producing bad taste and smell.
A substance like BHA added to food to prevent oxidation of fats and oils.
Filling a food packet with nitrogen gas to remove oxygen and prevent rancidity.
A sealed container that keeps atmospheric oxygen away from stored food.

sections.trick: Fight rancidity with NRA: Nitrogen flush, Refrigerate, Airtight. Nitrogen is the lazy gas that refuses to react with oil, and that laziness is exactly what food needs.
sections.examPointer: Why chips packets are flushed with nitrogen and listing methods to prevent rancidity have appeared in CBSE papers (2023, 2020); expect 2 marks or one MCQ.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is the correctly balanced equation for the burning of magnesium ribbon in air?
mcqs.explanation: Two Mg atoms and two O atoms must appear on each side, giving 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, which satisfies the law of conservation of mass.

mcqs.question: When an iron nail is dipped in copper sulphate solution, the colour of the solution changes from
mcqs.explanation: Iron displaces copper: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. The blue copper sulphate turns light green as ferrous sulphate forms and brown copper deposits on the nail.

mcqs.question: On strongly heating pale green ferrous sulphate crystals, the smell produced is of
mcqs.explanation: 2FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3; the sulphur oxides evolved smell of burning sulphur while the solid turns brown.

mcqs.question: In the electrolysis of water, the volume of gas collected at the cathode compared with that at the anode is
mcqs.explanation: Water splits as 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2, so hydrogen at the cathode is collected in double the volume of oxygen at the anode.

mcqs.question: White silver chloride kept in sunlight turns grey because of
mcqs.explanation: Sunlight decomposes silver chloride: 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2; the fine silver formed looks grey, which is the basis of black and white photography.

mcqs.question: When quicklime is added to water in a bucket, the reaction that follows is
mcqs.explanation: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 is a combination reaction in which a large amount of heat is released, so the bucket becomes hot.

mcqs.question: Brown fumes observed on strongly heating lead nitrate are due to the gas
mcqs.explanation: 2Pb(NO3)2 -> 2PbO + 4NO2 + O2; nitrogen dioxide is the brown gas, while the residue is yellow lead oxide.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a displacement reaction?
mcqs.explanation: Iron, being more reactive, displaces copper from its salt solution; the other options show double displacement, decomposition and combination respectively.

mcqs.question: When lead nitrate solution is mixed with potassium iodide solution, the precipitate formed is
mcqs.explanation: Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI -> PbI2 + 2KNO3; lead iodide separates as a bright yellow precipitate, a classic precipitation reaction.

mcqs.question: In the reaction between sodium sulphate and barium chloride solutions, the white precipitate obtained is of
mcqs.explanation: Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl; barium sulphate is insoluble in water and settles as a white precipitate.

mcqs.question: Respiration is considered an exothermic reaction because
options: Energy is released during the breakdown of glucose in cells
mcqs.explanation: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy; the slow combustion of glucose releases heat energy that maintains body temperature and powers life.

mcqs.question: When barium hydroxide is mixed with ammonium chloride in a test tube, the bottom of the tube feels cold. The reaction is therefore
mcqs.explanation: The mixture absorbs heat from the surroundings, lowering the tube temperature; absorption of heat defines an endothermic reaction.

mcqs.question: In the reaction MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2, the substance oxidised is
mcqs.explanation: HCl loses hydrogen to form Cl2, so it is oxidised; MnO2 gains hydrogen and is reduced to MnCl2.

mcqs.question: In the reaction SO2 + 2H2S -> 3S + 2H2O, sulphur dioxide behaves as
mcqs.explanation: SO2 loses oxygen to become sulphur, so it is reduced and hence acts as the oxidising agent, while H2S is oxidised.

mcqs.question: Packets of chips are flushed with nitrogen gas mainly to
options: Prevent oxidation of fats and oils
mcqs.explanation: Nitrogen is unreactive and replaces oxygen inside the packet, preventing rancidity caused by oxidation of fats and oils.

mcqs.question: The black coating formed on silver articles on long exposure to air is of
mcqs.explanation: Silver reacts with sulphur compounds in air to form a black layer of silver sulphide; this is corrosion of silver.

mcqs.question: Copper vessels acquire a green coating on exposure to moist air for long. This coating is of
mcqs.explanation: Copper reacts with moist carbon dioxide in air to form a green layer of basic copper carbonate, a form of corrosion.

mcqs.question: The reaction Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe, used for welding railway tracks, is an example of
mcqs.explanation: More reactive aluminium displaces iron from its oxide; so much heat is released that the iron produced is molten. This is the thermite reaction.

mcqs.question: A gas evolved when dilute sulphuric acid acts on zinc granules burns with a pop sound when a burning candle is brought near it. The gas is
mcqs.explanation: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2; the pop sound with a burning splinter is the confirmatory test for hydrogen gas.

mcqs.question: Which of the following equations is correctly balanced?
mcqs.explanation: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2 has equal Fe, O and H atoms on both sides and matches the product iron(II,III) oxide formed with steam.

boardQuestions.question: Balance the following chemical equations and identify the type of reaction in each case: (a) Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2 (b) CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 (c) Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + NaCl
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2; iron displaces hydrogen from steam, so it is a displacement reaction (iron is oxidised and hydrogen reduced). 2) (b) CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 on heating; a single compound breaks into two simpler substances, so it is a thermal decomposition reaction and is endothermic. 3) (c) Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl; the two compounds exchange ions and an insoluble white precipitate of barium sulphate forms, so it is a double displacement (precipitation) reaction. Marks are given for correct coefficients in each equation and one mark for correctly naming the type of each reaction.

boardQuestions.question: Why is respiration considered an exothermic reaction? Support your answer with the chemical equation.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) During respiration, glucose combines with oxygen inside the cells and breaks down, releasing energy in the form of heat which keeps the body warm and drives life processes. 2) Since heat energy is released along with the products, the reaction is exothermic. 3) Equation: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy. Any reaction that releases heat on forming its products, like this slow combustion of glucose, is classified as exothermic.

boardQuestions.question: A student heated a spatula full of pale green crystals in a dry test tube. The crystals first turned white and then a brown residue formed with a pungent smell. Identify the crystals, write the equation and name the type of reaction.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) The pale green crystals are ferrous sulphate, FeSO4.7H2O; heating first removes the water of crystallisation, turning them white. 2) On stronger heating the salt decomposes: 2FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3. 3) The brown residue is ferric oxide, Fe2O3, and the pungent smell of burning sulphur comes from the gases SO2 and SO3. 4) Since one substance breaks into three products on heating, this is a thermal decomposition reaction, and because heat is absorbed it is also endothermic. Writing the balanced equation, the colour observations and the type earns full marks.

boardQuestions.question: In the electrolysis of water experiment, why is a small amount of dilute sulphuric acid added? Which gas is collected in double volume and how is it tested? Name the type of reaction.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Pure water is a very poor conductor, so a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid are added to make it conducting by providing ions. 2) On passing current, water decomposes: 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2. Hydrogen is liberated at the cathode and oxygen at the anode, so hydrogen gas is collected in double the volume of oxygen, as the formula of water has hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2:1. 3) Hydrogen is tested by bringing a burning candle near the tube; it burns with a pop sound. 4) Since one compound splits into two elements using electricity, it is an electrolytic decomposition reaction and is endothermic in nature.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the chemistry of whitewashing a wall. Write the two equations involved and state why the wall acquires a shiny finish after two or three days.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) Quicklime, CaO, is added to water and slaked to give calcium hydroxide: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, releasing much heat, so this is an exothermic combination reaction. 2) The milky solution of slaked lime is applied to the walls. Calcium hydroxide reacts slowly with the carbon dioxide of air to form a thin layer of calcium carbonate on the walls: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O. 3) Calcium carbonate is a hard, white, lustrous substance, so after two or three days the wall acquires a shiny finish. The two balanced equations and the explanation of the CaCO3 layer carry the marks.

boardQuestions.question: Identify the substance oxidised, the substance reduced, the oxidising agent and the reducing agent in the following: (a) CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O (b) ZnO + C -> Zn + CO2 (c) MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) CuO loses oxygen and becomes Cu, so CuO is reduced and is the oxidising agent; H2 gains oxygen to become H2O, so H2 is oxidised and is the reducing agent. 2) (b) ZnO loses oxygen to become Zn, so ZnO is reduced and is the oxidising agent; carbon gains oxygen to form CO2, so C is oxidised and is the reducing agent. 3) (c) MnO2 gains hydrogen and is reduced to MnCl2, so MnO2 is the oxidising agent; HCl loses hydrogen to form Cl2, so HCl is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent. Remember the rule: the substance oxidised is always the reducing agent and the substance reduced is always the oxidising agent.

boardQuestions.question: Read the passage and answer: The iron gates of a house near the sea coast got covered with a brown flaky substance within a year, while the silver puja articles at home turned black and the copper vessel turned green. (a) Name the process affecting each object. (b) Write the condition and formula for the brown coating on iron. (c) Suggest two methods to protect the iron gate.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) All three objects show corrosion, the slow eating up of metal surfaces by substances in the atmosphere: iron shows rusting, silver forms black silver sulphide coating, and copper forms green basic copper carbonate coating. 2) (b) Rusting of iron needs both air (oxygen) and moisture together; neither alone can rust iron. The brown flaky deposit is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3.xH2O, where the number of water molecules is variable. Sea coast air is moist and salty, so rusting is faster there. 3) (c) The gate can be protected by painting it regularly so that air and moisture cannot touch the surface, or by galvanisation, that is coating it with a thin layer of zinc which does not rust and shields the iron. Oiling, greasing or chrome plating are also acceptable answers. 4) Silver blackens due to reaction with sulphur in air, and copper greens due to moist carbon dioxide; both are slower corrosion processes but follow the same principle of attack by the environment.

boardQuestions.question: What is rancidity? State any two methods by which rancidity of fried food can be prevented, with one reason each.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) When fats and oils in food are oxidised on long exposure to air, their taste and smell change; this spoilage is called rancidity. 2) Prevention methods: (a) flushing packets with nitrogen gas, because nitrogen is unreactive and replaces oxygen, stopping oxidation of the oil; (b) storing food in airtight containers, which cuts off contact with atmospheric oxygen. 3) Other valid answers: adding antioxidants like BHA, refrigeration, or keeping food away from sunlight. Any two methods with the correct reason of blocking oxidation earn full marks.

boardQuestions.question: Translate the following statements into balanced chemical equations and state the type of reaction in each: (a) Hydrogen gas combines with nitrogen to form ammonia. (b) Barium chloride reacts with aluminium sulphate to give aluminium chloride and a precipitate of barium sulphate. (c) Sodium metal reacts with water to give sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) 3H2 + N2 -> 2NH3; two substances combine to form a single product, so it is a combination reaction. 2) (b) 3BaCl2 + Al2(SO4)3 -> 2AlCl3 + 3BaSO4; the two salts exchange their ions and insoluble barium sulphate precipitates out, so it is a double displacement reaction, specifically a precipitation reaction. 3) (c) 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2; sodium displaces hydrogen from water because it is highly reactive, so it is a displacement reaction, and it is strongly exothermic, so much that the hydrogen evolved may catch fire. 4) While balancing, only coefficients are changed: three H2 molecules supply six H atoms for two NH3; three BaCl2 supply three Ba2+ for three BaSO4; two Na give two NaOH and one H2. Marks: one for each balanced equation and one each for correctly naming the type, plus presentation.

boardQuestions.question: Why are decomposition reactions called the opposite of combination reactions? Write one balanced equation of each type and state the energy relationship between them.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) In a combination reaction two or more substances form a single product (A + B -> AB), while in a decomposition reaction the same single substance breaks back into two or more products (AB -> A + B); the direction of change is exactly reversed, hence decomposition is the opposite of combination. 2) Example of combination: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, which releases heat, so it is exothermic. 3) Example of decomposition: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 on heating, which absorbs heat, so it is endothermic. 4) Generally combination reactions evolve energy while decomposition reactions need an input of heat, light or electricity, so the two classes are opposites both in the direction of the change and in the energy flow.
